subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which best describes the basic idea of a merge sort?
options: Repeatedly dividing the list into halves, then merging them in order
Trying every possible password
Checking each item from the start one at a time
Comparing adjacent items and swapping them
questions.explain: A merge sort repeatedly divides the list into halves and then merges them back together in order.

questions.q: In an insertion sort, what happens to each new item?
options: It is removed from the list
It is swapped with the very first item
It is compared only with the last item
It is placed into its correct position among the already-sorted items
questions.explain: An insertion sort takes each item and inserts it into its correct place within the sorted section.

questions.q: In computational thinking, what is decomposition?
options: Breaking a problem down into smaller, more manageable parts
Hiding unnecessary detail to focus on the main idea
Spotting patterns between problems
Writing the final program code
questions.explain: Decomposition means breaking a problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems.

questions.q: What does a binary search do at each step on a sorted list?
options: Checks the first item only
Swaps adjacent items that are out of order
Compares the middle item and discards half the list
Splits the list into single items and merges them
questions.explain: A binary search checks the middle item and discards the half that cannot contain the target.

questions.q: Consider the algorithm: x = 5, then x = x + 3, then x = x * 2. What is the final value of x?
questions.explain: x starts at 5, becomes 8 after adding 3, then becomes 16 after multiplying by 2.

questions.q: Why is a binary search usually more efficient than a linear search on a large sorted list?
options: It uses less memory than any other method
It checks every item twice
It does not need the list to be sorted
It halves the number of items to search each step
questions.explain: A binary search halves the remaining items each step, so it needs far fewer comparisons on large lists.

questions.q: What is abstraction in computational thinking?
options: Breaking a problem into smaller parts
Removing or hiding unnecessary detail to focus on what matters
Testing a program with boundary data
Repeating a set of instructions
questions.explain: Abstraction is removing unnecessary detail to focus on the important parts of a problem.

questions.q: Which is a valid definition of an algorithm?
options: A high-level programming language
A type of network protocol
A sequence of steps to solve a problem or complete a task
A piece of hardware that stores data
questions.explain: An algorithm is a sequence of steps that solves a problem or completes a task.

questions.q: What does pattern recognition mean in computational thinking?
options: Splitting a problem into smaller parts
Identifying similarities or common features between problems
Writing the program in machine code
Hiding unnecessary detail
questions.explain: Pattern recognition is spotting similarities or shared features between problems so solutions can be reused.

questions.q: On a list of 8 sorted items, what is the maximum number of comparisons a binary search needs?
questions.explain: Binary search on 8 items needs at most 4 comparisons in the worst case: floor(log2(8)) + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4.

questions.q: What does 'algorithmic thinking' mean?
options: Drawing a network diagram
Choosing the cheapest hardware
Working out the steps needed to solve a problem
Hiding unnecessary detail
questions.explain: Algorithmic thinking is identifying the ordered steps required to solve a problem.

questions.q: An algorithm contains: count = 0, then a loop 'WHILE count < 3: count = count + 1'. How many times does the loop body run?
options: Infinitely
questions.explain: The body runs for count values 0, 1 and 2, incrementing to 3, so it runs three times before the condition fails.

questions.q: Which best describes how a bubble sort works?
options: It splits the list in half repeatedly and merges
It inserts each item into its correct position in a sorted part
It searches for the largest item only once
It repeatedly compares adjacent items and swaps them if out of order
questions.explain: A bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent items and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.

questions.q: Pseudocode is best described as:
options: A type of flowchart
The machine code produced by a compiler
A structured way of describing an algorithm in plain language
A specific programming language that computers run directly
questions.explain: Pseudocode describes an algorithm using structured plain language, not a real programming language.

questions.q: What does a parallelogram usually represent in a flowchart?
options: Input or output
A start or stop
A decision
A process
questions.explain: A parallelogram represents an input or output in a flowchart.

questions.q: After one full pass of a bubble sort on [5, 3, 8, 1] (comparing and swapping adjacent items), which value is guaranteed to be in its final position?
options: 1, at the start
8, at the end
3, at the start
5, in the middle
questions.explain: Each bubble sort pass moves the largest remaining value to the end, so after one pass 8 is in its final position.

questions.q: A linear search is performed on the unsorted list [4, 9, 2, 7] for the value 2. How many items are checked before it is found?
questions.explain: Checking from the start, 4 then 9 then 2, the value 2 is found on the third item checked.

questions.q: What does the efficiency of an algorithm usually measure?
options: How well it uses resources such as time and memory
How many programmers wrote it
How colourful the flowchart is
Whether it is written in a high-level language
questions.explain: Efficiency measures how well an algorithm uses resources, mainly time taken and memory used.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a trace table?
options: To draw a flowchart automatically
To translate code into machine code
To record the values of variables as an algorithm is followed step by step
To store a program permanently
questions.explain: A trace table records how variable values change as you step through an algorithm.

questions.q: Which of these is a key requirement for a binary search to work?
options: The list must be stored in a database
The list must be sorted
The list must contain only numbers
The list must be unsorted
questions.explain: A binary search only works on a list that is already sorted.

questions.q: How does a linear search find an item?
options: By checking each item in turn from the start until found
By jumping straight to the middle item
By repeatedly halving the search area
By sorting the list first every time
questions.explain: A linear search checks each item in turn from the beginning until the target is found.

questions.q: Which symbol shape in a flowchart represents a decision?
options: A rectangle
A diamond
An oval
A parallelogram
questions.explain: A diamond (rhombus) represents a decision in a flowchart.
